posts.title: The MMSE middle band says nothing about capacity
posts.insight: In a JAMA review of treatment-decision capacity, MMSE scores of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood of incapacity; only scores below 20 or above 24 shifted it, and even a high score does not rule incapacity out.
posts.angle: Practitioners still write a score beside a capacity judgement. The pooled evidence shows the middle band is uninformative, so a decision-specific assessment is always needed.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the score bands are an empirical finding (Sessums 2011); 'use the score to prompt, never to replace, an assessment' is clinical interpretation consistent with decision-specific capacity.

captions.x:
An MMSE score of 20 to 24 gives no information about whether a patient can make a treatment decision.

A JAMA review of 43 studies of treatment-decision capacity in adult medical patients (Sessums 2011) found scores below 20 made incapacity more likely (likelihood ratio 6.3). Scores of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood (0.87). Scores above 24 made it less likely (0.14).

The MMSE was not designed to assess capacity. A high score lowers the chance that someone lacks capacity; it does not rule it out.

Capacity is judged one decision at a time. Use the score to prompt an assessment, never to replace it.
captions.linkedin:
An MMSE score of 20 to 24 gives no information about whether a patient can make a treatment decision.

A JAMA Rational Clinical Examination review pooled 43 high-quality prospective studies of capacity for treatment decisions in adult medical patients (Sessums, Zembrzuska and Jackson, 2011).

The MMSE result came in three bands:

1. Below 20: incapacity more likely (likelihood ratio 6.3).
2. 20 to 24: no change in likelihood (likelihood ratio 0.87).
3. Above 24: incapacity less likely (likelihood ratio 0.14).

The authors concluded the MMSE is useful only at extreme scores. It was not designed to assess capacity.

An earlier study of 37 people with Alzheimer's disease found a similar pattern: scores of 21 to 25 did not reliably separate people who could consent from those who could not. That study was small and looked at consent to research, so treat it as support rather than the main evidence.

The same review found about 1 in 4 medical inpatients lacked capacity for a treatment decision, and clinicians recognised it in about 4 in 10 of those patients.

Three practical points follow.

A high score lowers the chance of incapacity but does not rule it out. A person can still lack capacity for a complex decision.

These cut-offs belong to the MMSE. Do not carry them over to the MoCA or ACE-III.

Capacity is judged one decision at a time. A score can prompt an assessment of the decision in front of you; it can't replace one. The Aid to Capacity Evaluation had useful accuracy in the review and is free to use.
captions.bluesky:
An MMSE of 20 to 24 did not change the likelihood that a patient lacked capacity for a treatment decision (JAMA review, 43 studies). Below 20 made it more likely; above 24 less likely, but not ruled out.

The MMSE was not built for capacity. Assess the decision itself.

posts.title: Elderspeak and resistance to care
posts.insight: Elderspeak is usually meant kindly, yet in filmed dementia care it was followed by resistance far more often than adult talk, and three one-hour staff sessions reduced it in a small trial.
posts.angle: Recognise the phrases without blame, then treat elderspeak as a care-quality problem that a short training course changed.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the observational link and trial results are empirical (Williams 2009, 2017; Shaw 2022); 'treat it as a care-quality problem' is a clinical and ethical judgement.

captions.x:
'Sweetheart', 'good girl', 'are we ready for our bath?' Staff usually say these things to be kind. The name for it is elderspeak: talking to an older adult the way people talk to a small child, often in a high, sing-song voice.

In a US study that filmed 80 care episodes with 20 nursing home residents with dementia, resistance to care followed elderspeak about 55 times in 100, against about 26 in 100 after ordinary adult talk. That is a link, not proof of cause.

A small trial in 13 US nursing homes then gave staff three one-hour sessions. Elderspeak fell from about 35% of care time by about 14 percentage points, and resistance fell by about 15 points. At three months the drop in elderspeak held; the drop in resistance was no longer statistically clear.

We should treat elderspeak as a care-quality problem with a tested remedy.
captions.linkedin:
'Sweetheart', 'good girl', 'are we ready for our bath?', 'you want to get up now, don't you?'

Most staff who talk like this mean it kindly, or are trying to get care done. The name for it is elderspeak: talking to an older adult the way people talk to a small child, with pet names, 'we' instead of 'you', questions that answer themselves, and a high, sing-song voice. Older people who are asked mostly find it patronising.

The evidence links it with resistance to care in people with dementia.

In a US study that filmed 80 care episodes with 20 nursing home residents, resistance followed elderspeak about 55 times in 100, compared with about 26 in 100 after ordinary adult talk. This is a link in the moment, not proof of cause, and ordinary adult talk was uncommon in the recordings.

In a US hospital study of 88 care encounters with 16 people with dementia, 85 included some elderspeak. Encounters with less elderspeak were less likely to include refusal. Pain was linked with refusal too.

Then a test of change. In a cluster randomised trial in 13 US nursing homes (27 residents), staff had three one-hour sessions. Elderspeak fell from about 35% of recorded care time by about 14 percentage points. Resistance fell from about 36% of care time by about 15 points, in step with the fall in elderspeak. At three months, the drop in elderspeak held at 12 points; the 13-point drop in resistance was no longer statistically clear. Without training, neither changed.

The trial was small, lost many participants, and only half of staff attended all three sessions.

My reading: elderspeak is ordinary kindness that misfires. We should treat it as a care-quality problem with a tested remedy, and teach the adult alternative: the person's name, a real choice, and saying what you are about to do.
captions.bluesky:
Pet names and 'shall we' talk (elderspeak) were followed by resistance to care about 55 times in 100 in filmed dementia care, against 26 after adult talk: a link, not proof.

In a small nursing home trial, three one-hour staff sessions cut elderspeak.
captions.threads:
Elderspeak means talking to an older adult as to a small child: pet names, 'we' for 'you', a sing-song voice. It is usually meant kindly.

In filmed dementia care, resistance followed it about 55 times in 100, against 26 after adult talk. That is a link, not proof.

In a small trial in 13 US nursing homes, three one-hour staff sessions cut elderspeak by about 14 percentage points of care time. A matching fall in resistance was no longer clear at three months.

posts.title: Going with a parent to the doctor without taking over
posts.insight: When a companion asks the older person questions, prompts them to speak and asks their view, the older person is more likely to take an active part in decisions.
posts.angle: Families can help most by helping the person speak for themselves, and can agree roles before the appointment.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the link between companion behaviour and patient involvement is empirical (Clayman 2005, association); agreeing roles beforehand is practical advice consistent with a review, not a tested intervention.

captions.x:
At your parent's appointment, one of the most useful things you can do is ask them a question: what do you think?

Nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical appointments bring someone, most often a husband, wife or grown-up child.

In a US study that filmed 93 GP visits by people aged 65 to 95 who came with a relative or friend, patients took a more active part in decisions when the companion asked them questions, prompted them to speak and asked their view. It looked at one visit each, so it shows a link, not proof of cause.

Before you go in, agree what your parent wants to say themselves and what they want you to add. Then let them answer first.
captions.linkedin:
At your parent's appointment, one of the most useful things you can do is ask them a question: what do you think?

Nearly 4 in 10 adults at routine medical appointments bring someone with them, according to a review of 13 studies. Most often it is a husband, wife or grown-up child. The people who bring someone are, on average, older and in poorer health.

Companions help in real ways. Appointments were longer, and doctors gave more medical information, when someone came along.

But the older person can drift out of the conversation. In a small US study of 30 first appointments, older patients who came with someone raised fewer topics themselves and were often left out of the talk.

What the companion does seems to count. In a US study that filmed 93 GP visits by people aged 65 to 95 who came with a relative or friend, patients were more likely to take an active part in decisions when the companion asked them questions, prompted them to speak and asked what they thought. The study looked at one visit each, so it shows a link, not proof that the companion's behaviour caused the difference.

A review of 52 studies found companions were often seen as helpful, while taking over or making demands was seen as less helpful. People differed widely in how much they wanted a companion to do.

So, before the appointment:

1. Ask your parent what they want to say themselves, and what they want you to add.
2. Sit where they can see both you and the doctor.
3. When a question comes, let them answer first.
4. Write down what was decided.

If you are the one being accompanied, you can tell your companion which job you want them to do.
captions.bluesky:
Going to the doctor with a parent? Ask them: what do you think?

In a US study of 93 GP visits, older patients took a more active part in decisions when their companion prompted them to speak and asked their view (a link, not proof).

Agree beforehand who says what.
captions.threads:

posts.title: Teach-back: what 18 trials found
posts.insight: A 2026 review of 18 randomised trials found no clear effect of teach-back on patients' knowledge, with low or very low certainty evidence of better confidence and self-reported short-term adherence.
posts.angle: Teach-back is often taught as a method that works; the randomised evidence is much less sure. Its best use may be as a check on the clinician's explanation.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the trial findings are empirical (Vick 2026); using teach-back as a check on your own explanation is professional judgement.

captions.x:
Eighteen randomised trials of teach-back, with about 2,000 people, found no clear effect on what patients knew afterwards.

Teach-back means asking patients to explain in their own words what they have been told. It is often taught as a method that works: an earlier review reported benefit in 19 of 20 studies of mixed design.

The 2026 review included only randomised trials and graded certainty. The knowledge evidence was very low certainty and too varied to pool. Confidence and self-reported short-term adherence improved, at low or very low certainty.

No clear effect differs from no effect: the question is open. My view: keep using teach-back to check your own explanation, and stop describing it as shown to improve knowledge.
captions.linkedin:
Eighteen randomised trials of teach-back, with about 2,000 people, found no clear effect on what patients knew afterwards.

Teach-back means asking patients to explain in their own words what they have been told. It is often taught as a method that works. An earlier review (Talevski 2020) reported benefit in 19 of 20 studies, of mixed design.

The 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis by Vick and colleagues in the Journal of General Internal Medicine included only randomised trials and graded the certainty of each result.

Knowledge: 9 trials measured it. They were too different to combine, there was no clear pattern, and certainty was very low.

Confidence in managing health: improved, very low certainty.

Self-reported adherence in the short term: improved, low certainty. The size of both effects was very uncertain.

Two limits on the scope. The review covered teach-back in a single encounter, not longer education programmes that include it. The trials were in adults generally, not older people specifically.

No clear effect differs from no effect. This is an evidence gap, and it should be described as one.

Older patients have a particular stake. In a study of 260 people with cancer, older patients recalled less than younger ones when a lot of information was given; how much was said, and how serious the news was, were stronger guides than age alone.

My view: keep using teach-back, as a test of your own explanation. When the patient's account comes back with gaps, the gaps show what you need to say again, more simply or with less at once. Stop describing it as shown to improve knowledge.
captions.bluesky:
A 2026 review of 18 randomised trials found no clear effect of teach-back on what patients knew afterwards (very low certainty). Confidence and short-term adherence improved, at low certainty.

Use teach-back to check your explanation; don't sell it as shown to work.
captions.threads:
Teach-back, asking patients to explain back what they were told, is often taught as a method that works.

A 2026 review of 18 randomised trials found no clear effect on what patients knew afterwards, at very low certainty. Confidence and self-reported short-term adherence improved, at low or very low certainty.

That is an open question, not a failure. Keep using teach-back to find what your explanation missed.

posts.title: Talking Mats: two studies, two answers
posts.insight: In one small study couples felt more involved with Talking Mats, but a 2026 randomised trial found no clear difference from ordinary care-planning talks, with high involvement in both groups.
posts.angle: A picture-based tool can structure a conversation, but the evidence does not show it beats a careful ordinary conversation. Whatever method is used, ask the person with dementia directly.
posts.position_basis: mixed: study results are empirical (Murphy and Oliver 2013; Bangsbo 2026; Collins 2023); 'ask the person with dementia directly' is an ethical judgement.

captions.x:
Talking Mats is a tool that uses picture cards on a mat to help people with dementia talk about daily life. Two studies give different answers about what it adds.

In one small study, 18 couples living with dementia talked twice, once with the mats and once as usual. Both partners said they felt more involved with the mats. The study was not randomised and was led by the tool's developers.

In a 2026 Swedish trial, 101 older people with dementia in home care were randomly assigned to care-planning talks with or without the mats. Both groups rated their involvement high, and the trial did not show a clear difference.

Whatever method is used, we should ask the person with dementia directly, and not only the family.
captions.linkedin:
Talking Mats is a tool that uses picture cards on a mat to help people with dementia talk about daily life. Two studies give different answers about what it adds.

The first was small. 18 couples living with dementia talked about daily life twice, once with the mats and once as usual. Both partners said they felt more involved when they used the mats. The study was not randomised, involved one visit, and was led by the tool's developers.

The second was a randomised trial. In Swedish home care, 101 older people with dementia were randomly assigned to care-planning talks with or without Talking Mats. Both groups rated their involvement high, and the trial did not show a clear difference between them.

That null result needs careful reading. High scores in both groups left little room to show a difference. The same staff ran both kinds of talk. Staff had a two-day course, and some used the mats only once. So the trial did not show a benefit; it did not show the mats are useless either.

A review of ways to hear the views of people with more advanced dementia found that each tool had some use, and none had clear evidence over the others.

My reading: a structured, visual way of asking can help some conversations. The evidence does not show it beats a careful ordinary conversation.

What the studies share is the aim. We should ask the person with dementia about their own daily life, directly, whatever method is used, and not rely only on the family's account.
captions.bluesky:
Talking Mats uses picture cards to help people with dementia talk about daily life. In a small study, couples felt more involved with it. A 2026 trial of 101 people found no clear difference from usual talks.

Whatever the method, ask the person with dementia directly.
captions.threads:
Talking Mats uses picture cards on a mat to help people with dementia talk about daily life.

In a small study, 18 couples felt more involved with the mats. In a 2026 Swedish trial, 101 people with dementia rated involvement high with or without them, and the trial showed no clear difference.

So the tool may help some conversations, but it has not been shown to beat a careful ordinary one. Whatever the method, ask the person with dementia directly.

posts.title: For many Deaf signers, pen and paper is a second language
posts.insight: Many Deaf people who sign grew up with BSL as their first language, so written notes are an unreliable substitute for a qualified BSL interpreter in health conversations.
posts.angle: Deaf BSL users face poorer communication and signs of worse care; booking a qualified interpreter for important conversations is the service's job.
posts.position_basis: mixed: communication barriers and blood pressure findings are empirical (Rogers 2025; Emond 2015; Terry 2024; Lesch 2019); 'booking is the service's job' and 'ask for an interpreter' are ethical and practical judgements supported by secondary legal sources.

captions.x:
Many Deaf people who sign grew up with British Sign Language as their first language. For some, written English is a second language.

BSL has its own grammar. Notes full of medical words can be hard to follow, and research with Deaf patients finds that handing over pen and paper often does not fix the problem.

Deaf patients describe interpreters not being booked, being asked to bring a relative, and relatives leaving things out. For older Deaf people, patchy access to interpreters risks treatment without proper consent.

In a UK health check of 298 Deaf BSL users, 37 in 100 had a high blood pressure reading, against 21 in 100 in an English population survey.

For any talk about diagnosis, treatment, consent or discharge, ask for a qualified BSL interpreter. Booking one is the service's job.
captions.linkedin:
Many Deaf people who sign grew up with British Sign Language as their first language. For some, written English is a second language.

BSL is a language in its own right, with its own grammar. Notes full of medical words can be hard to follow. A scoping review of 51 studies of Deaf sign language users' experience as patients, and UK research with Deaf patients, find that handing over pen and paper often does not fix the problem.

Deaf patients describe interpreters not being booked, being asked to bring a relative instead, and relatives leaving things out. A review of research on older Deaf people who sign found that patchy access to interpreters puts them at risk of treatment without proper consent.

There are signs of the cost. In a UK health check of 298 Deaf BSL users aged 20 to 82, 37 in 100 had a high blood pressure reading, against 21 in 100 in an English population survey. The researchers linked this to poor communication with health services. That is their interpretation of an association, not a measured cause.

What services should do follows from this.

In England, NHS and social care services must record a person's communication needs and meet them, and any BSL interpreter they use must be qualified. Across the UK, the Equality Act expects services to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people, including in how they communicate.

If you are Deaf and use BSL, or you support someone who does: for any conversation about diagnosis, treatment, consent or discharge, ask the service to book a qualified BSL interpreter. Booking one is the service's job, not yours. Some people prefer a family member for a particular appointment, and that choice should be respected.

posts.title: Aphasia and capacity: give a way to answer
posts.insight: People with aphasia after a stroke may keep their judgement while losing words; word-heavy decision tasks disadvantage them, so involve a speech and language therapist before the capacity conversation.
posts.angle: Capacity assessments rely on talk, which puts people with aphasia at risk of being judged unable when the problem is language. Speech and language therapists can help but report not being asked.
posts.position_basis: mixed: aphasia frequency, word-task disadvantage and the survey barrier are empirical; 'ask the speech and language therapist before the capacity conversation' is clinical judgement consistent with the legal duty to take practicable steps.

captions.x:
After a stroke, some people lose words but may keep their judgement.

About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia, a difficulty understanding or using language. In a study of 16 people with aphasia, they struggled most when a decision task relied on words, especially explaining their reasons aloud.

Some people with aphasia also have problems with memory or reasoning. The answer comes from a supported assessment, not from the diagnosis.

Supports that can help include key words written down, pictures of the options and more time. In a 2026 survey of 195 speech and language therapists, one barrier they reported was that other professionals did not ask for their help.

Before the capacity conversation, ask the speech and language therapist.
captions.linkedin:
After a stroke, some people lose words but may keep their judgement.

About 1 in 3 people in hospital after a stroke have aphasia, a difficulty understanding or using language. The figure varies by stroke type and timing.

A capacity assessment asks a person to understand information, weigh it and communicate a choice, and most assessments do this through talk. That puts people with aphasia at a disadvantage. In a study of 16 people with aphasia, they struggled most when a decision task relied on words, especially explaining their reasons aloud. On decision tasks without words, they did not score clearly differently from people without aphasia. The study was small and used laboratory tasks, not real assessments.

Aphasia can hide a person's ability to decide. Some people with aphasia also have problems with memory or reasoning, so the answer comes from a supported assessment, not from the diagnosis.

Research on people with aphasia after stroke describes supports that can help:

1. Key words written down.
2. Pictures of the options.
3. Trained conversation partners.
4. More time.

Their effects have not been tested one by one.

In England and Wales the law says a person can't be treated as unable to decide until all practicable steps to help them have failed. In Scotland, a communication difficulty that can be overcome with help or aids does not count as incapacity.

Speech and language therapists can help set this up. In a 2026 survey of 195 speech and language therapists in 32 countries, one barrier they reported was that other professionals did not ask for their help with decisions.

Before the capacity conversation, ask the speech and language therapist.

posts.title: Say it again, one idea at a time
posts.insight: For people with Alzheimer's disease, simple sentences and saying things again helped understanding in small studies, while slowing down on its own did not; plain wording differs from elderspeak.
posts.angle: Carers can use simple, repeated sentences without sliding into child-like talk; the line between them is pet names, sing-song voice and 'shall we'.
posts.position_basis: empirical finding (Small 1997, Small 2003, Kemper and Harden 1999) with a definition from a concept analysis (Shaw and Gordon 2021); no position beyond practical advice.

captions.x:
In a small experiment with 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, saying a sentence again, in the same or different words, helped them understand it. Saying it more slowly did not.

A study that recorded 18 couples at home found something similar: simple sentences worked, and slowing down did not. Simple means one idea per sentence.

If you care for someone with Alzheimer's, plain wording is ordinary adult speech. Elderspeak is different: pet names such as 'love' or 'sweetheart', a high sing-song voice, and 'shall we' that makes the choice for the person.

These were small, older studies. A calm pace is fine; it just did not help on its own. If the person is hard of hearing, face them and speak clearly.
captions.linkedin:
In a small experiment with 15 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease, saying a sentence again, in the same or different words, helped them understand it. Saying it more slowly did not.

A second study recorded 18 couples at home, one partner with Alzheimer's disease, while they did everyday tasks. Simple sentences worked, and slowing down did not. Simple means grammatically simple, with one idea per sentence, rather than just fewer words.

Experiments with older adults without dementia point the same way. Keeping each sentence to one idea, and adding a word of explanation, helped. A high, sing-song voice did not help, and made people report more trouble following.

If you care for someone with Alzheimer's, it helps to know where plain wording ends and elderspeak begins.

Plain wording is ordinary adult speech: one idea per sentence, saying it again, and checking you were understood.

Elderspeak is talking to an older adult as if to a small child. It adds pet names such as 'love' or 'sweetheart', a high sing-song voice, and 'we' or 'shall we' that makes the choice for the person.

So: 'Your daughter is coming at two. She is coming at two o'clock.' Illustrative example. Not: 'Shall we get ready for our visitor, sweetheart?'

These were small studies (15 people; 18 couples) from the 1990s and 2000s. Slowing down on its own did not help in them; that does not make a calm pace wrong.

If the person is also hard of hearing, face them and speak clearly. Clear is different from high-pitched or sing-song.

posts.title: Ask for the clinic letter to be written to you
posts.insight: National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges recommends that hospital doctors write clinic letters to the patient, yet at one large eye hospital about 2 in 100 were.
posts.angle: The letter is usually written about you to your GP; you can ask for it to be written to you, and national guidance supports that.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the guidance and letter audit figures are empirical or documentary; 'you can ask' is practical advice.

captions.x:
'Could you write the letter to me, please?' You can ask this at the end of a hospital clinic appointment.

Many people already get a copy of their clinic letter, but it is usually written to the GP and about them. National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) recommends that hospital doctors write outpatient clinic letters to the patient.

At one large London eye hospital, researchers analysed 4.6 million clinic letters from 2013 to 2025. About 2 in 100 were written to the patient. About 95 in 100 were harder to read than recommended for patients.

This is professional guidance, not law. If your letters go to your GP, ask whether the next one could be written to you.
captions.linkedin:
'Could you write the letter to me, please?' You can ask this at the end of a hospital clinic appointment.

After most clinic visits a letter is written. Many people already get a copy, but it is usually written to the GP and about them.

National guidance from the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges (2018) recommends that hospital doctors write outpatient clinic letters to the patient, rather than about the patient to the GP.

Practice has been slow to follow. At one large London eye hospital, researchers analysed 4.6 million clinic letters written between 2013 and 2025. About 2 in 100 were written to the patient. About 95 in 100 were harder to read than the level recommended for patients.

Two cautions about that study. It is one eye hospital, with patients of all ages, so it does not describe every clinic. And 'written to the patient' was judged by a computer rule that counts uses of 'you' and 'your', which the authors call imperfect.

Patients seem to want the change. In a survey at one English hospital clinic, 42 of 80 patients wanted letters written to them, 4 wanted them written to their GP, and the rest had no preference.

This is professional guidance, not law, and the doctor can decide how to write. But you can ask.

If you have a clinic appointment coming up, ask at the end: 'Could you write the letter to me, please?' If a relative comes with you, they can ask too.

posts.title: Put the real options to the person
posts.insight: A person can only weigh the options they have been told about; a capacity assessment about going home must set out the realistic options and the help attached to each.
posts.angle: A bare 'Can you manage at home?' tests the person against options nobody has described. A Court of Protection judge and residence-capacity specialists say to present detailed options.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the CC v KK ruling and specialist recommendation are documentary; the study of ward practice is empirical (Emmett 2013); calling a bare question an unfair test is ethical and clinical judgement.

captions.x:
Before you assess whether someone can decide to go home, tell them what going home would involve.

In a 2012 Court of Protection case in England (CC v KK), an 82-year-old woman with dementia wanted to go home from a nursing home. Professionals had repeatedly judged that she lacked capacity to decide where to live. The judge found that she had it.

The judge said: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed."

Specialists recommend setting out each option and what it could mean: home with carers several times a day, with no guarantee, or a care home that may become permanent.

A bare 'Can you manage at home?' asks the person to weigh options nobody has described. We should not call that a fair test.
captions.linkedin:
Before you assess whether someone can decide to go home, tell them what going home would involve.

In a 2012 Court of Protection case in England (CC v KK), an 82-year-old woman with dementia wanted to go home from a nursing home. Professionals had repeatedly judged that she lacked capacity to decide where to live. The judge found that she had it.

The judge said: "The person under evaluation must be presented with detailed options so that their capacity to weigh up those options can be fairly assessed." (para 68)

The same judge warned that professionals can slip from asking whether she could decide into asking what was best for her.

This is one first-instance ruling in England and Wales. It binds no other court, and Scotland has different legislation. But its reasoning applies to any capacity assessment.

Specialists in residence capacity recommend telling the person:

1. Why a move is suggested.
2. What the other options are, such as going home with carers several times a day.
3. What each choice could mean, including that a care home may become permanent and that going home with help carries no guarantee.

Practice has varied. A study on English hospital wards found staff varied widely in what information they gave or tested when judging whether a person with dementia could decide where to live. When researchers filmed four capacity assessments in hospital, in people with acquired brain injury, options were not always put to the patient.

A bare 'Can you manage at home?' asks the person to weigh options nobody has described. In my view that is an unfair test of their ability. Describe the options, with the help attached to each, and then see whether the person can weigh them.

"Can you manage at home?" is a poor capacity question if nobody has said what help would be there.

posts.title: How often relatives predict your wishes
posts.insight: Relatives predicting a person's answers to imagined end-of-life treatment questions matched about 2 times in 3; informal talks did not improve this, but a structured, recorded planning conversation did.
posts.angle: Relatives are useful but fallible guides; write down your views and reasons and go through them in a structured way.
posts.position_basis: mixed: accuracy figures and the trial are empirical (Shalowitz 2006; Kirchhoff 2010); 'write down your views and go through them' and 'ask relatives what the person valued' are clinical and ethical judgements.

captions.x:
Would the person who would speak for you give the answer you would give?

A 2006 review of 16 studies asked people and their relatives the same questions about imagined treatment near the end of life. Relatives gave the same answer as the person about 2 times in 3, and a different answer about 1 time in 3.

Relatives the person had chosen were no more accurate than next of kin. Families who said they had talked about it were no more accurate either, in those studies of ordinary conversations.

A structured conversation did help. In a US trial with 313 people with heart or kidney disease, a planning talk led by a trained professional, ending in a written record of the person's goals, left relatives understanding those goals much better than usual care.

Write down your views and your reasons while you can, and go through them with the person who would speak for you.
captions.linkedin:
Would the person who would speak for you give the answer you would give?

A 2006 systematic review pooled 16 studies in which people, and the relative who would speak for them, answered the same questions about treatment near the end of life. The relatives gave the same answer as the person about 2 times in 3, and a different answer about 1 time in 3.

These were imagined situations, not real decisions, and the figure is across answers rather than a score for each relative.

Two findings may surprise families. Relatives the person had chosen were no more accurate than next of kin. And families who said they had talked about it beforehand were no more accurate than those who had not. That applies to ordinary, unstructured conversations.

A structured conversation is a different thing. In a US trial with 313 people with heart failure or kidney disease and the relatives who would speak for them, a planning conversation led by a trained professional, ending in a written record of the person's goals, left relatives with a much better understanding of those goals than usual care.

For you, if you are thinking ahead: write down your views and your reasons while you can. Then go through them with the person who would speak for you, with a professional's help if you can get it.

For clinicians: when a person can't decide, ask relatives what the person valued and what they said, not only what they think the person would choose.

More posts in the Reading the evidence series take one study at a time and say what it shows and what it leaves open.

captions.threads:
In a review of 16 studies, relatives predicting a person's answers to imagined end-of-life treatment questions matched about 2 times in 3.

Being chosen, or having chatted about it, did not make them more accurate. In a US trial, a structured planning talk with a trained professional and a written record helped relatives understand the person's goals much better.

Write down your views and reasons, and go through them with the person who would speak for you.

posts.follow_note: Includes the one follow invitation in this set: the Reading the evidence series.
posts.verification_notes: Shalowitz 2006 abstract: 68% of 19,526 paired answers, 16 studies, hypothetical scenarios, designation and prior discussion no better; 'mostly US' omitted. Kirchhoff 2010 abstract: 313 pairs, facilitated, written record, much better understanding (no kappa). Liu 2024 listed as supporting source for structured planning, not quoted. 'Ordinary conversations' qualification carried.
